tagline: Up the old turnpike to the war's highest Union camp.
intro: Near Cheat Bridge a short piece of the old Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike leaves US 250 and switchbacks up the side of Cheat Mountain to White Top, a knob at 4,085 feet. It is about three miles, a quarter hour's drive.

In July 1861 Union troops began a fort on the summit to hold the turnpike, which crossed about 100 feet below it. It was the highest Union camp of the war. Snow was reported on August 13, and horses froze to death in the middle of September. The garrison left in April 1862, and one Indiana soldier hoped it was their last look at Cheat Mountain.

moments.title: Cheat Bridge
moments.text: Coming back more than 40 years after his service here, Ambrose Bierce found the old covered bridge over Shavers Fork still carved all over with soldiers' names.

moments.title: Cheat Summit Fort
moments.text: Trails and an overlook interpret the earthworks of the camp, and just south of them the hollows of the soldiers' emptied graves still show in the ground.

practical: The turnpike beyond the fort is impassable, so the backway comes back down to US 250 by the signed Cheat Summit Fort road. The road is sometimes closed by snow.
